newsitem.title: UK: Sterling steady but off highs vs mark in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Sterling steady but off highs vs mark in Europe.

text.p: Sterling was on a firm footing against the dollar and mark at Europe's midday, with cable in particular supported by the dollar's overall weakness.
However, sterling/mark was slightly dampened by renewed speculation over Britain's re-entry into the European exchange rate mechanism.

This was sparked by a comment by Gavyn Davies, managing director at Goldman Sachs International, who told a conference here that if sterling rejoined the ERM at 2.50-2.60 marks with 15-percent fluctuation bands, this would capture all the movements in sterling over the past six years.

However Davies -- also Goldman's chief international economist who is widely tipped to become a deputy governor at the Bank of England -- added that achieving such a level would be hard, and that it would be dangerous for Britain to rejoin the ERM at the moment.
"Davies' suggestion that 2.50-2.60 could be the ERM re-entry level took sterling/mark down a bit, and this also took cable down. But the move wasn't that big," said one UK bank trader.
The pound was at 2.7905/15 marks at 1145 GMT after touching a session high of 2.8040 earlier, but was still above its late Tuesday European level of 2.7853/63.

It was at $1.6550/60 against its late Tuesday level of $1.6440/50, supported by the dollar's softening across the board after the Federal Reserve decided to leave key U.S. interest rates on hold on Tuesday.
Analysts said the pound also got encouragement from some comments by Bank of England governor Eddie George about pre-empting UK inflation.

"Eddie George's comments have helped (sterling), since he warned about acting to pre-empt inflation and said he saw inflationary pressures building up this year and the year after," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell here.
"So the market's confirmed that we're going to see higher interest rates this year," he said.

George told BBC radio this morning the short-term outlook for Britain's inflation was encouraging, but added that the central bank was more concerned about containing inflationary pressures that might be building up in the longer term.
And minutes of the UK monetary meeting on April 10, released today, showed George had told then Chancellor Kenneth Clarke that he saw significant risk of inflation overshooting two years ahead.

Expectations of higher rates offset the potential negative impact of another comment by George, contained in the central bank's annual report issued today, that sterling's strength posed a "genuine dilemma" for monetary policy.

"There was nothing too surprising in that comment. The market thinks they will raise rates anyhow, regardless of the fact that sterling is strong, because we will see inflationary pressure coming through eventually," Barr said.
